Weighted averages of predicted means: standardisation and post-stratification

Source: R/ilm_average.R, R/zzz-iml-aliases.R
ilm_average.Rd

Averages a prediction of the mean over groups of its rows, with weights, draw by draw. With the rows a reference population and equal weights, it is standardisation: the population's average mean under the model, for example with a covariate set to each of several values. With the rows population cells and their sizes as weights, it is post-stratification (as in multilevel regression and post-stratification, MRP).

Usage

ilm_average(pred, by = NULL, weights = NULL)

Arguments

pred

A prediction of the mean, from ilm_predict() or ilm_forecast() with target = "mean".

by

Names of columns in the prediction's rows, as as.data.frame() shows them. There is one average for each combination of their values. NULL, the default, averages every row. Rows of different scenarios are never averaged together.

weights

The rows' weights: a non-negative number per row, or the name of a column in the prediction's rows. They are normalised within each group, so only their ratios matter. NULL, the default, weights the rows equally.

Value

A prediction of the mean (see The prediction object in ilm_predict()), with one row per combination of by (and of scenario), n_rows, the number of rows each average combines, and weight, their total weight.

Details

The average is taken within each draw, so its uncertainty is the joint uncertainty of the rows' means: whatever they share within a draw (the parameters, a unit's effect) carries into the average.

Post-stratification weights each cell's predicted mean by the cell's population count, as Gelman and Hill (2007) do for state opinion from national polls (section 14.1, equation (14.1)); their code in the same section computes the weighted average in each simulation draw, as here.

Means, not new observations

Standardisation and post-stratification average what the model expects, so pred must be a prediction of the mean (target = "mean"). A weighted average of new observations is a different question, whose answer depends on the sizes of the groups being averaged. For an unweighted average of new observations, use ilm_aggregate() with fun = "mean".

References

Gelman, A. and Hill, J. (2007). Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models. Cambridge University Press. Section 14.1, "State-level opinions from national polls": equation (14.1), and the weighted average computed in each simulation draw.

See also

ilm_predict() with target = "mean" for the rows' means; ilm_aggregate() for totals, and averages of new observations.

Examples

set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(clinic = factor(rep(sprintf("c%02d", 1:20), each = 10)),
                age = rep(c("young", "old"), 100), x = rnorm(200))
d$visits <- rpois(200, exp(0.5 + 0.4 * d$x + 0.3 * (d$age == "old") +
                           rnorm(20, 0, 0.4)[d$clinic]))
fit <- illume::ilm_model(visits ~ x + age + (1 | clinic), data = d,
                         family = "poisson", verbose = FALSE)
## post-stratification: the mean for a population that is 70% old (the
## population average does not use the clinic, but the rows need its column)
cells <- data.frame(age = c("young", "old"), x = 0, size = c(300, 700), clinic = NA)
p <- ilm_predict(fit, cells, target = "mean", groups = "population", nsim = 500)
as.data.frame(ilm_average(p, weights = "size"))
#>   n_rows weight estimate     mean lower_0.9 upper_0.9
#> 1      2   1000 2.604135 2.645949  2.211712  3.192428
